learn.title: The Duck Curve: Solar's Sunset Challenge
learn.intro: The duck curve describes how solar generation peaks at midday then plunges at sunset, forcing grids to ramp up other sources exactly when demand rises. This mismatch is one of the biggest grid management challenges of the energy transition, requiring flexible storage and dispatchable resources.
learn.c1_text: Plot net load (demand minus solar) over 24 hours and you get a belly-drooping curve resembling a duck. In California, midday net demand can drop by over 12 GW in spring, then surge back up as solar fades and people arrive home. It looks weird until you see it.
learn.c2_text: Traditional baseload plants like coal and nuclear can't ramp up fast enough. Operators must curtail solar midday, then fire up gas peakers by 6 PM. The steep evening ramp — sometimes 15 GW in three hours — stresses every generator, transmission line, and market pricing mechanism on the system.
learn.c3_text: India's duck curve is forming fast. With 90+ GW of solar installed and RE targets of 500 GW by 2030, states like Rajasthan and Gujarat already see duck-shaped demand curves. The CEA forecasts evening ramps exceeding 20 GW, pushing battery storage tenders and RTC renewable policy in 2024-25.
learn.stat1: California duck curve: net demand can swing ~12 GW between 1 PM and 7 PM
learn.stat2: India solar installed capacity crossed 90 GW in 2024
learn.stat3: California curtailed ~2.4 TWh of solar in 2022 due to duck curve effects

learn.title: Floating Offshore Wind for Deep Waters
learn.intro: Floating offshore wind unlocks deep-water sites beyond 60m depth where fixed-bottom turbines are uneconomic. With 80% of global offshore wind potential in deep waters, floating platforms are essential to scale wind energy massively, especially in countries like India, Japan, and the US west coast.
learn.c1_text: Engineers use three main platforms. Spar buoys look like giant floating cylinders anchored by chains, used by Hywind Scotland. Semi-submersibles sit on submerged pontoons — most common design. Tension-leg platforms (TLPs) use vertical tethers, like a buoy. Each balances cost, stability, and assembly complexity differently.
learn.c2_text: Floating turbines connect to seabed via 3-9 chain or synthetic mooring lines, holding position in 30m waves. Dynamic cables carry power to the seabed, handling constant motion. Semi-subs and TLPs reduce steel by 20-30% versus spar designs, but each is optimised for water depth and seabed geology.
learn.c3_text: India identified 174 GW of offshore wind potential along Tamil Nadu and Gujarat. Fixed turbines work near coast, but floating opens deeper Gulf of Khambhat and Gulf of Mannar sites. The MNRE demonstration project targets 4 GW floating wind off Tamil Nadu, with viability gap funding under consideration.

learn.title: Hydrogen Colours Explained: Blue Green Grey
learn.intro: Hydrogen is colour-coded by how it is made. Green hydrogen uses renewable electricity to split water, blue uses fossil fuels with carbon capture, and grey is the dirty default. Understanding the palette is essential to evaluate hydrogen's true climate impact and project economics.
learn.c1_text: Made by electrolysing water with renewable electricity. Zero direct emissions, but needs cheap solar/wind. Cost: $3-6/kg today, expected to fall below $2/kg by 2030. Think of it as solar energy stored as gas — versatile for steel, ammonia, trucks, and shipping fuel.
learn.c2_text: Grey hydrogen comes from steam-methane reforming of natural gas, producing ~10 kg CO2 per kg H2. Blue adds carbon capture and storage (CCS), capturing 90-95% of emissions but costing 30-50% more. Neither is zero-carbon long-term, but blue bridges the gap while renewables scale up.
learn.c3_text: India launched its National Green Hydrogen Mission in January 2023 with $2.3 billion outlay, targeting 5 million tonnes annual production by 2030. The SIGHT programme subsidises electrolysers. Reliance has committed to a 100% green hydrogen plant in Jamnagar — potentially the world's largest integrated facility.
learn.stat1: Grey hydrogen emits ~10 kg CO2 per kg H2 produced
learn.stat2: Green hydrogen cost: $3-6/kg in 2024, target below $2/kg by 2030
learn.stat3: India targets 5 million tonnes green H2 production by 2030
learn.stat4: Blue hydrogen captures 90-95% of CO2 emissions via CCS technology

learn.title: Flow Batteries for Grid-Scale Storage
learn.intro: Flow batteries store energy in liquid electrolyte tanks, not solid electrodes. Power and energy scale independently, making them ideal for 6-12 hour grid storage. Vanadium and iron chemistries offer decades-long lifespans, low fire risk, and near-100% depth-of-discharge, complementing lithium-ion's strength.
learn.c1_text: Two electrolyte liquids — one positive, one negative — flow through a cell stack where ions cross a membrane, generating electricity. Tank size determines energy capacity; stack size determines power. Add bigger tanks later without replacing the stack — like a fuel cell you can refuel.
learn.c2_text: Vanadium redox batteries (VRFB) use the same element in both tanks, eliminating cross-contamination — the proven workhorse with 20,000+ cycle life. Iron flow batteries use cheap iron salts but lower energy density. VRFB costs ~$300-500/kWh, declining steadily with Chinese manufacturers entering the market.
learn.c3_text: India's first commercial vanadium flow battery is a 400 MWh project by Tata Power in 2024, likely Asia's largest. The Ministry of Power's 4-hour RTC tender framework favours flow batteries for long-duration storage. State utilities like NTPC are piloting 5 MWh iron-flow systems for solar smoothing.
learn.stat1: Vanadium flow batteries: 20,000+ cycles with minimal degradation
learn.stat2: Tata Power commissioning 400 MWh VRFB in India (2024)
learn.stat4: Lithium-ion typically delivers 4,000-6,000 cycles vs flow's 20,000+

learn.title: Offshore Wind: Design to Grid
learn.intro: Offshore wind farms are engineering marvels: 15 MW turbines on monopiles or jackets, strung together by inter-array cables, and exporting power via high-voltage subsea cables to onshore substations. The full chain from seabed foundation to grid connection is complex, capital-intensive, and rapidly evolving.
learn.c1_text: In waters up to 60m, monopiles — single steel cylinders — are hammered into the seabed. Deeper sites use jackets, four-legged lattice structures anchored with piles. Today's largest offshore turbines (Vestas V236, Siemens SG 14-222) produce 15 MW, enough clean power for ~18,000 homes annually.
learn.c2_text: Inter-array cables link turbines at 33-66 kV. Offshore substations step up voltage to 132-220 kV for export. High-voltage AC is used within 80 km of shore; beyond that, HVDC converter stations minimise losses. A single 1 GW farm may have 200+ km of subsea cable plus two giant substations.
learn.c3_text: India awarded its first offshore wind tender in 2022 for 4 GW off Gujarat. Vishakapatnam and Tamil Nadu follow. SECI has signed PPAs at ₹3.5/unit. Challenges include high subsea cable costs, monsoon logistics, and port infrastructure. The country targets 30 GW offshore wind by 2030 under updated NDC commitments.

learn.stat2: Modern offshore turbines reach 15 MW rated capacity

learn.title: Wind Turbine Lifespan and Blade Recycling
learn.intro: Wind turbines last 20-25 years, but their massive composite blades are hard to recycle. With 14,000 tonnes of blade waste expected globally by 2050, the industry is racing to develop recycling technologies. End-of-life management is now central to wind's sustainability story and circular economy plans.
learn.c1_text: Blades are made of glass or carbon fibre reinforced with epoxy or polyester resin — thermoset composites that don't melt or reshape easily. A single 80m blade weighs 35-50 tonnes. Landfill dominates today, but EU regulations now ban blade disposal, forcing manufacturers like Vestas and GE into recycling partnerships.
learn.c2_text: Mechanical recycling shreds blades into filler for cement. Thermal processes burn resin to recover fibres. Solvolysis uses chemicals to dissolve resin at low temperatures, recovering pristine fibres for new blades. Siemens Gamesa pioneered a fully recyclable blade in 2021, and GE is scaling its thermoplastic blade tech.
learn.c3_text: India's first wave of wind turbines installed in the 1990s-2000s is now approaching end-of-life. With 47 GW of installed wind, decommissioning will hit 4-6 GW per year by 2030. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy is drafting blade recycling guidelines, and Suzlon is exploring recycled composite supply chains.
